2. uv end to end uv replaces pyenv, venv, pip, pip-tools, pipx and Poetry with one binary.

The root page's Toolchain atlas replays the first five commands ( uv init , uv add , uv run , ruff, pytest); this section covers what you need after that: interpreters, the kinds of project, what uv sync really does, extras and groups, scripts, tools, workspaces and the pip interface.

Interpreters uv downloads standalone CPython builds (from the python-build-standalone project) instead of using whatever the system has. uv python install 3.14 3.14t 3.15 installed every interpreter used on this page; t is the free-threaded build.

Since uv 0.13.0 (2026-10-09) the default is 3.15: uv python install with no version, or a project with no pin, gets 3.15 (an existing compatible interpreter is still used); uv python pin 3.14 keeps you on 3.14 while a dependency lacks 3.15 wheels.
In Python you would have run pyenv install and then pointed a venv at it; with uv, --python 3.15 on any command is enough, and a project's .python-version file pins it.

Three kinds of project Since uv 0.12, plain uv init and uv init --app both make a packaged application: code under src/ , a console script, and the uv_build backend (so uv run app-demo works). --no-package gives the old flat layout with a main.py , and --lib makes a library with a py.typed marker (it tells type checkers the package ships annotations).
Correction to the old page The old "zero to expert" page said uv init myproj , uv add requests , uv run main.py .
With uv 0.12.23 plain uv init creates no main.py (output above); run the console script with uv run <project-name> , or create the flat layout with uv init --app --no-package .
The root page records the same correction.

The three files that must agree A uv project is three things: pyproject.toml (what you asked for: ranges), uv.lock (what one resolution picked: exact versions and hashes for every platform at once, which is what "universal lock" means) and .venv (what is installed). uv add , uv lock and uv sync move them back into agreement, and uv run syncs before it runs.
Step through a real session: Every command and output is the real one from src/pb/uvwalk/walk_uv.sh , run with uv 0.12.23 on 2026-10-05.
What the session shows: uv sync is exact : it removes anything the lock does not ask for in this sync, which is why orjson (an extra) disappeared until --extra fast was given.

Use --inexact to keep extra packages. uv run is the opposite: it installs what is missing but removes nothing unless you pass --exact ( uv docs: locking and syncing ). --locked refuses a stale lock : the build fails instead of silently resolving new versions.
Use it in CI. --frozen goes further and installs from the lock without checking pyproject.toml at all.
Dependency groups ( [dependency-groups] , PEP 735, here dev ) are for you, never published; extras ( [project.optional-dependencies] ) are for your users ( pip install tokcount[fast] ).
The dev group is installed by default; --no-dev leaves it out.
The system python3 cannot import httpx : the project's packages live in .venv .

That is what uv run does that bare python does not: sync, then run inside the project environment, no activation needed. uv tree shows why each package is there; uv export writes a requirements.txt for tools that need one, or the standard pylock.toml (PEP 751, accepted in 2025), the first lock format every installer can share.
Scripts with their dependencies inside (PEP 723) A one-file script can declare its own dependencies in a comment block; uv run script.py then builds a cached throwaway environment for it.
This replaced "make a venv for this one script".
Tools: uvx is pipx uvx tool@version runs a command-line tool in its own cached environment without installing it into your project; uv tool install puts it on your PATH.
Every type checker on this page was run this way, pinned to an exact version.

Workspaces: several packages, one lock A workspace is a repository with several packages (a library and the CLI that uses it, say) that share one uv.lock and one .venv , like a Cargo workspace in Rust. { workspace = true } makes the CLI depend on the library's source, not on a PyPI release.
The pip interface For old repositories and Dockerfiles, uv venv and uv pip install behave like python -m venv and pip, only faster; nothing is locked unless you ask ( uv pip compile ).

How much faster, measured The same three packages (httpx, pydantic, rich and their dependencies) into a fresh Python 3.14 environment, three runs each with hyperfine (network included, so treat these as rough): What uv costs, and when not to use it uv is one company's tool (Astral, which announced on 2026-03-19 that it is joining OpenAI, per the Astral blog ); the code is open source under MIT and Apache-2.0.
Its lock format is its own, though it can export the standard pylock.toml .
Where a project needs non-Python binaries (a specific CUDA toolkit, MKL, GDAL), conda or pixi still solve a problem uv does not.
And in a repository that already uses Poetry, switching tools is a team decision, not a drive-by change.
Common mistakes with uv Running python script.py instead of uv run script.py and wondering why imports fail: the project environment is not active.
Editing pyproject.toml by hand and forgetting uv lock : CI with --locked catches it (the error above).
Not committing uv.lock for an application: every machine then resolves on its own day.
Putting test tools in [project.optional-dependencies] : they are then published as an extra; use a dependency group.
Expecting uv sync to leave packages you installed by hand with uv pip install : it removes them.

3. ruff: lint and format A linter reads your code without running it and reports likely bugs and style problems; a formatter rewrites layout (spacing, line breaks, quotes) so nobody argues about it. ruff does both, in Rust, and replaced flake8 and its plugins, isort, pyupgrade and black.

Here is a file with eight problems you have probably written yourself: New in ruff 0.16 (2026-07-23): the default set grew from 59 to 413 rules That is why the first run already reports isort (I), pyupgrade (UP), bugbear (B), simplify (SIM) and bandit (S) findings with no configuration at all.

The release also removed 18 pycodestyle and pyflakes rules from the default set, among them E711 ( == None ) and E401 (two imports on one line), which is why those two appear only once they are selected explicitly below ( ruff changelog ).
Pin ruff in your dev group, or one upgrade can fail every CI run. --fix applied nine safe fixes (sorted and pruned imports, list for List , str | None for Optional[str] , the empty f-string).

The five that remain need a human: a mutable default argument ( seen=[] is created once and shared by every call), a file opened without with and never closed, a try / except / pass that ruff suggests writing as contextlib.suppress , a bare except that also swallows KeyboardInterrupt , and == None (use is None ). "Unsafe" fixes ( --unsafe-fixes ) are the ones that can change behaviour, so ruff never applies them silently.

A small starting configuration in pyproject.toml (written for this page, not run as shown): [tool.ruff] target-version = "py314" # lets UP rules rewrite to the newest syntax you support line-length = 100 [tool.ruff.lint] extend-select = ["E711", "E401"] # add back what 0.16 removed, if you want it ignore = ["S101"] # assert is fine in tests What it costs Nothing at run time.
The cost is noise: a large default rule set on an old codebase reports hundreds of findings.
Adopt it with ruff check --add-noqa once (it writes suppression comments for existing findings) and fix new code only, or start from an explicit select list.

5. pytest essentials pytest finds files named test_*.py , runs every function named test_* , and treats a plain assert as the check.

Five features cover most real test suites; all five are in this one file, testing the root page's token-counting rule: Fixtures ( chat_file , defined in conftest.py so every test file can use it) are set-up functions that pytest calls for you when a test names them as a parameter.

Built-in ones: tmp_path (a fresh folder per test) and monkeypatch (set an environment variable or attribute, undone after the test). @pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test per row of inputs, each reported separately. pytest.raises asserts that a block raises a given exception.
Subtests (new in pytest 9.0, 2025-11-05) check several values inside one test and report each failure separately, for cases where the values are only known at run time.

Configuration now lives natively in pyproject.toml under [tool.pytest] (pytest 9.0; the older [tool.pytest.ini_options] table still works), and strict = true turns on every strictness option (unknown markers and config keys become errors).
The u marks are the two passing subtests.
Now a test with a wrong belief in it.

Predict what pytest prints before you reveal it: That message is pytest's assertion rewriting : at import time it rewrites each assert in test files so that a failure shows the values of every sub-expression ( where 2 = tokens('max_tokens') ).

This is why pytest needs no assertEqual family. -k selects tests by name, --co lists what would run (note the parametrize ids, with non-ASCII escaped), and -n 4 from the pytest-xdist plugin spreads tests over four worker processes.
On nine tests the workers' start-up makes it slower (0.37 s against 0.01 s); it pays off on suites that take minutes.
Common mistakes with pytest Testing implementation details (private functions, exact call counts) instead of behaviour, so every refactor breaks tests that found no bug.
A fixture with scope="session" that returns a mutable object: one test's change leaks into the next.
Forgetting that test files are imported: module-level code in a test file runs at collection time, even for tests you deselected.

Lazy imports (3.15), measured A Python program's start-up time is mostly imports: each import finds a file, loads or compiles its bytecode and runs all its top-level code, including its own imports.
A command-line tool that imports httpx, pydantic and rich at the top pays for all three even when the user only asked for --help .
Until now the fix was to move imports inside functions.

3.15 adds lazy import : the name is bound to a lightweight proxy and the module loads the first time the name is used. import argparse lazy import httpx # was: import httpx lazy import pydantic # was: import pydantic lazy from rich.console import Console # was: from rich.console import Console That is the only change between the two files measured below ( src/pb/lazy/ ).
Both run the fast path, count "hello world" , which needs none of the three libraries.

Step through what Python imports, to scale: Eager imports lazy import Eager file, -X lazy_imports=all What to take from it: the lazy file loads , and the global switch -X lazy_imports=all (or PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS=all ) gets the same result without editing the file.
The work has not disappeared: a run that uses httpx pays for it at the first use instead.
What it costs, and when not to use it Errors move: a misspelled module raises at first use, not at start-up; the traceback shows both places.
Import side effects (a plugin registering itself, logging configured at import) happen later or never.
Do not make such imports lazy; the global all mode can be filtered with sys.set_lazy_imports_filter .
Only at module level: lazy inside a function, a class body or a try block is a SyntaxError , and so is lazy from x import * .
Code that must also run on 3.14 or older cannot use the keyword (it is a SyntaxError there; see the Version explorer ); list the modules in __lazy_modules__ instead, which older versions ignore.
The PEP and the release disagree on one detail PEP 810 (status Final) describes three global modes, normal , all and none (none would force every import eager, for debugging).
3.15.0rc3 accepts only two, as What's New says: Use normal to undo all ; there is no switch that forces explicit lazy imports eager.

Free-threading in practice The GIL (global interpreter lock) is the lock in the standard CPython build that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time; threads still help when they wait on I/O, but CPU-bound threads take turns ( Part 1 explains threads and the GIL from the start).
The free-threaded build removes it (PEP 703): experimental in 3.13, officially supported but still optional in 3.14 (PEP 779), installed separately as python3.14t ( uv python install 3.14t ).
Check which one you are on with sys._is_gil_enabled() .

The workload below is the root page's program: count tokens per user over 100,000 JSONL chat lines (the root's generator, seed 7), split across threads, each thread filling its own Counter that the main thread merges ( src/pb/ft/ ).

Every thread recorded when it finished each block of 1,000 lines; this is that recording, to scale, for four threads: 3.14, GIL 3.14t, no GIL 3.15rc3, GIL 3.15rc3t, no GIL Speed-up over one thread on the same interpreter, median of five runs.
The Runtime lab has every run, 1 to 8 threads, and the single-thread overhead.
Part 1 timed a different CPU-bound job on 3.14t (0.94 s serial, 0.37 s on four threads, about 2.5x); this final run of the token counter measured with four threads, under a heavier load.
Both are rough: on a busy laptop the same job varies by tens of percent between runs.
The bug the GIL was hiding (and was not preventing) Now the same four threads update one shared dictionary instead of their own: shared[user] = shared.get(user, 0) + n .
That line reads, adds and writes back in three steps; if two threads read the same old value, one addition is lost.
Python's documentation never promised that a read-modify-write like this is atomic under the GIL ( Python FAQ ); the GIL only made losing an update rare.
Without the GIL the same bug happens on most runs.
What the free-threaded build does guarantee is that built-in objects stay internally consistent: the dictionary never crashes or corrupts, it only holds the wrong totals.
The fixes are the same on both builds: a threading.Lock around the update (exact in every run above), or, better, no shared state, which is what the scaling run did.
Will your dependencies run without the GIL?
A C, C++ or Rust extension must declare that it is safe without the GIL.
If it does not, importing it on the free-threaded build silently turns the GIL back on for the whole process, with a warning.
Real output from two tiny C extensions, identical except for one line that declares support ( Py_mod_gil ): -X gil=0 (or PYTHON_GIL=0 ) forces it off anyway, at your own risk.
Packages that have not been ported may also refuse to build.

What it costs, and when not to use it Single-thread speed.
The 3.13 HOWTO measured about 40% overhead; for 3.14, What's New says "roughly 5-10%" and the 3.14 HOWTO "about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux" (pyperformance).
Measured here on one workload: see the Runtime lab .
PEP 779 set a 20% memory overhead target for phase II; this page did not measure memory.
Your own thread safety.
Races that the GIL made rare now happen; audit shared mutable state before switching.
One unported extension turns the GIL back on for everyone (above).
Not for I/O-bound work : threads already overlap waiting under the GIL, and asyncio is the usual tool for many connections.
Whether the free-threaded build ever becomes the default ("phase III") is "left for a future PEP" (PEP 779); the old page's forecast of 3.16 to 3.17 is a guess, not a plan.
Corrections to the old page "~3x speedups on 4-core CPU-bound thread pools": no source given.

section: 10. the experimental jit, on and off
text: The experimental JIT, on and off A JIT (just-in-time compiler) turns hot code into machine code while the program runs.

section: 10. the experimental jit, on and off
text: CPython's (PEP 744, since 3.13) is a copy-and-patch JIT: when the specialising interpreter finds a hot loop, it records a trace of its micro-operations and stitches together machine-code templates ("stencils") that were compiled with LLVM when CPython itself was built, so you need no LLVM at run time.

section: 10. the experimental jit, on and off
text: It ships compiled into the official macOS and Windows installers and the uv builds used here, but is off unless you set PYTHON_JIT=1 ; in 3.14 and later, sys._jit.is_enabled() tells you whether it is on.

section: 10. the experimental jit, on and off

section: 10. the experimental jit, on and off
text: It is off by default in 3.15 too, and a 2x speed-up of a Python loop is still far from moving the loop to NumPy or Rust (the root's Benchmark tab measures the token counter in all four languages).
Subinterpreters (3.14), measured A subinterpreter is a second, isolated Python interpreter inside the same process: its own modules, its own globals and, since 3.12, its own GIL (PEP 684).
3.14 exposed them in the standard library (PEP 734): concurrent.interpreters and InterpreterPoolExecutor , which has the same interface as the thread and process pools.

They sit between threads and processes: parallel on the normal GIL build like processes, but cheaper to start, and like processes they share nothing by default: arguments and results cross by pickling, except immutable built-ins (None, bool, bytes, str, int, float and tuples of these), which are shared or copied cheaply, and memoryview and interpreter queues, which really share mutable data ( docs ). from concurrent.futures import InterpreterPoolExecutor with InterpreterPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as ex: totals = list(ex.map(count_slice, parts)) # same code as with ThreadPoolExecutor On this job, subinterpreters and processes both clearly beat threads on the GIL build, because each worker has its own GIL; processes were somewhat faster here.
Neither reached 4x with 4 workers: each worker receives 25,000 lines by pickling and returns a pickled Counter , and the machine was busy.
A new subinterpreter started more than ten times faster than a spawned process, and about a hundred times slower than a thread.
The mistake everyone makes first: a subinterpreter has its own sys.path , so a module the main interpreter found through a sys.path.insert is invisible to it.

Simple arguments can hide this; a list argument has to be pickled together with the function, and then it fails: What it costs, and when not to use it Every extension module must opt in to being loaded in several interpreters, and the most important one has not: Objects cannot be shared, only copied; and on the free-threaded build plain threads already run in parallel with shared memory.
Use them on the normal build for CPU-bound work whose inputs and outputs are small, when process start-up is the problem.
